title: LG Energy Solution signs MoU with US startup Indigotech - electrive.com
content:
Commercial Vehicles
LG Energy Solution has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with Indigotech, a US startup in the commercial electric vehicle sector. The collaboration aims to explore 46-Series cylindrical battery supply for commercial electric vans in the United States.
Image: LG Energy Solutions
Under the terms of the memorandum of understanding,
LG Energy Solution
Indigotech
will work toward a definitive agreement under which LG Energy Solution will supply 46-series cylindrical NCM battery cells for Indigotech’s upcoming “Flow Ride” and “Flow Cargo” electric vehicles from 2027 to 2030.
IndiGOtech is headquartered in Woburn,
Massachusetts
, a hot spot for electric mobility in the USA. The American startup specialises in electrifying commercial van platforms for the North American market and is developing an ecosystem that integrates vehicles, charging infrastructure, and digital services. The startup and the South Korean battery giant are targeting support for joint business development through vehicle-battery integration and performance verification efforts.
The two companies want to maximise vehicle performance by reviewing “opportunities to extend driving range and reduce charging times,” according to a statement from LG.
“Urban ride hail and delivery must electrify and automate at scale, but today’s electric vehicles are not designed for purpose, and are severely limited by the local charging infrastructure ― that’s why [the] vast majority of rides and deliveries are still driven by gas vehicles,” said Will Graylin, Chairman and CEO of indiGOtech. “Working toward a long-term relationship with LG Energy Solution brings together advanced battery technology for durable economic advantage for vehicles, drivers and fleet operators.”
For LG Energy Solution, the pending agreement is an opportunity to strengthen its competitiveness by securing additional customers for its 46-series cylindrical batteries in North America. According to the company, cylindrical battery shipments increased by 1.5 times year on year as of Q2. This was supported by what the company says was “stable mass production and expanded deliveries of its 46-series batteries.”
“Based on LG Energy Solution’s 46-series NCM cylindrical battery technology that boasts high energy density and rapid charging capabilities, we will closely collaborate with indiGOtech, which is successfully building the Transportation-as-a-Service (TaaS) ecosystem in the U.S.,” said Sunghwan Oh, Mobility & IT Battery Marketing Group Leader of LG Energy Solution. “Leveraging this partnership, we plan to enter the diverse commercial vehicle market in the U.S., including logistics, last-mile delivery, and ride-hailing.”

title: CATL opens largest Ning Service Centre outside Asia in Oslo - electrive.com
content:
CATL has opened its largest Ning Service Center outside Asia in Oslo. The new location will serve Norway and the Nordic region with battery testing, maintenance, repair, second-life applications, and recycling.
The new Ning Service Center in Oslo covers 8,000 square meters.
Image: CATL
A new battery lifecycle service centre operated by the Chinese battery giant CATL was opened in Oslo on 24 September. At 8,000 square metres, the facility is CATL’s largest Ning Service centre outside Asia and is intended to serve as a central hub for Norway and the other Nordic countries.
According to the company, the range of services includes diagnostics, maintenance, and repair, as well as insurance services, second-life applications, and recycling. Ning Service is designed to cover not only vehicle batteries but also applications in energy storage and robotics. The centre will also serve as a sales and experience hub for additional electric applications such as ships and eVTOL aircraft.
The expansion comes at a time when
already has a highly developed electric vehicle market. In August, the share of battery-electric passenger cars among new registrations was 98.7 per cent, according to CATL, while for buses and coaches it exceeded 60 per cent. With the growing and increasingly ageing vehicle fleet, the demand for battery diagnostics, repair, and condition assessment is also rising.
Data from the used car market also shows that a complete battery replacement is not always necessary. An analysis published this summer by Swedish dealer Carla, based on nearly 10,000 battery tests, found that many electric cars still retain a high proportion of their original battery capacity even after more than
100,000 kilometres
. This increases the importance of diagnostics and targeted repairs to extend battery life as long as possible.
CATL focuses on repair over battery replacement
This is precisely the focus of Ning Service’s business model. CATL aims to shift the aftermarket from complete battery replacement towards repair. According to the company, the processing time for complex repairs has been reduced from 72 to 48 hours.
Representatives from CATL and partners at the opening of the new Ning Service centre in Oslo.
The repair expertise currently covers 76.8 per cent of electric vehicle models. One of the tools used is the so-called “Intelligent Eagle Eye System”, which, according to CATL, is already in use in more than 150 repair workshops and ensures traceability and quality control.
The Oslo location is also set to become Ning Service’s most important training centre in the Nordic countries. CATL plans to offer certified courses and practical training for local technicians there. This is based on a training network across 39 European countries and a team of 14 experienced instructors. Collaborations with Norwegian universities and technical institutions are also planned.
“Customers are at the heart of everything we do at NING SERVICE. Working closely with our local partners, we will provide reliable battery lifecycle services that meet the needs of Norway’s EV market and support its continued electrification,” said Bruce Li, President of Quality Systems, Aftermarket Business Division, CATL.
The circular economy is also part of the concept. Together with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, CATL has launched the
Global Energy Circularity Commitment
initiative. Batteries are to be used for as long as possible, and the materials they contain are then to be recycled for use in new batteries.
CATL has been expanding Ning Service into an international aftermarket network for several years. The service business has existed since 2015, and Ning has operated as an independent brand since 2024. At the beginning of 2026, CATL opened its first Ning Service Experience Center in the Middle East in
. The facility there covers more than 7,000 square metres and also offers diagnostics, repair, maintenance, recycling, training, as well as logistics and storage services.
At 8,000 square metres, the new European location in Oslo is even larger. Ning Service currently operates a total of 1,394 service locations in 85 countries and regions. By 2027, CATL aims to have a presence in 100 countries, and by 2030, the network is expected to grow to 10,000 service locations.

title: 'Toyota Battery Center in North America' opens in Michigan - electrive.com
content:
Toyota USA has opened a battery development centre in the US state of Michigan. The Toyota Battery Center of North America (TBC) in Saline is set to strengthen the automaker's battery testing and evaluation capabilities across the spectrum of electric vehicle batteries in the Japanese automotive company's "Multi-Path Strategy".
Image: Toyota
Toyota USA has announced that its new facility will provide Michigan-based battery teams with expanded capabilities for battery evaluation and development. The centre is said to cover all technologies across the entire battery development cycle from raw material procurement to customer applications and recycling. The approximately 2,800-square-metre facility is described by Toyota as a “central hub” intended to support its North American production network.
This network currently includes a
battery plant in North Carolina
, which opened in 2025, and several vehicle manufacturing plants across North America. The new battery plant is the first of its kind outside Japan. Located near the small town of Liberty, it is the twelfth manufacturing facility that the Japanese automotive giant has built in the US. Toyota stated that the investment for the plant, announced last year, amounts to 14 billion euros and that a total of 5,100 jobs are expected to be created at the site.
Toyota continues to pursue a multi-path electrification strategy, with its signature hybrids still playing a significant role, as well as hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, which also require small batteries. This means batteries for full hybrids, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles will be tested, developed and evaluated at the Liberty plant. Toyota often refers to this approach as its “Multi-Path Strategy”, aiming to offer customers “a broad spectrum of sustainable mobility solutions”.
At the new development centre, Toyota teams will work in parallel on multiple new technologies for use in hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and battery-electric vehicles. “For Toyota customers, this facility means Toyota engineers can detect and resolve field concerns faster and closer to the source,” said Jordan Choby, Group Vice President of Powertrain. “It also means we can develop longer-lasting batteries designed to perform in the conditions American drivers face every day.”
Toyota also intends to open the facility to third parties, partnering with the University of Michigan’s Electric Vehicle Center. As a founding member of the Electric Vehicle Center, Toyota aims to underscore its commitment to training the next generation of battery engineers and technicians in Michigan through this programme.
“Toyota has long been at the forefront of battery development,” said Keita Moritsu, Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer, Toyota Motor North America R&D. “This center is where that leadership expands to North America — and where we’re building its next chapter.”

title: Data Center Batteries Shift to Active Power Role
content:
Stationary Batteries
Market Analysis
Design & Manufacturing
AI workloads and total cost of ownership priorities drive 16.2% annual growth as operators shift from backup to active power management.
October 5, 2026
4 Min Read
The sun is rising on battery energy storage systems such as those needed to power data centers.
Young777 / iStock via Getty Images
At a Glance
Data center battery market projected to reach $4.27 billion by 2035 with 16.2% annual growth rate
AI training jobs create power spikes reaching 10% of total facility capacity within seconds of demand
Lithium iron phosphate chemistry gains adoption over NMC due to superior thermal stability in facilities
The data center battery energy storage market is experiencing dramatic transformation as artificial intelligence workloads and operational economics reshape infrastructure priorities. According to the 2026 Data Center Energy Storage Industry Insights Report surveying 150 global professionals, 84% of operators now consider total cost of ownership (TCO) a top priority when selecting energy storage systems, while 57% identify higher power-density requirements and smaller footprints as major AI-driven impacts.
DataM Intelligence projects the global market will surge from $952.3 million in 2025 to $4.27 billion by 2035, representing 16.2% compound annual growth. North America leads with 40.2% market share, while Asia-Pacific emerges as the fastest-growing region. Lithium-ion batteries captured approximately 67% of 2025 market share, driven by migration from lead-acid systems and demand for higher energy density with lower maintenance.
Related:
Battery Technology’s Role in AI Growth and Innovation
Batteries now serve as active power buffers, not just backup
The fundamental shift extends beyond market statistics. As
Battery Technology reported from The Battery Show North America 2025
, the era of treating batteries as passive backup systems has ended. AI workloads force data centers to deploy advanced battery systems as active power buffers rather than emergency solutions. Data centers
highlight numerous conference sessions on AI at the 2026 Battery Show
in Detroit next week.
Traditional data center racks consumed two to 10 kilowatts with predictable demand that conventional UPS systems easily managed. AI training jobs now demand entire supercomputer capacity instantly, creating power spikes of 2% to 10% of total facility capacity within seconds. This unpredictable variability forces operators to deploy large-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) that draw grid power at steady rates, store it, and discharge rapidly during AI training spikes.
Strategic partnerships and manufacturing expansion are accelerating deployment
Recent collaborations underscore market evolution. Vertiv and CPower's April 2026 partnership integrates Vertiv's EnergyCore Grid BESS with CPower's virtual power plant platform, enabling behind-the-meter storage for demand response, resilience, and grid services. Major players including Schneider Electric, Eaton, ABB, Huawei Digital Power, and Delta Electronics compete as operators transition toward intelligent energy-management architectures.
Cummins secured its largest BESS contract
for a U.S. data center, deploying a 5 MWh LFP battery system managing AI workloads while addressing community concerns about diesel generator noise and emissions. The system features liquid cooling, flexible DC architecture compatible with multiple power conversion and energy management systems, and bridge-to-grid capability for integration with backup generators.
Related:
La Verne Battery Fire Evacuates 500—New Tech Could Stop the Next One
Cummins' LFP battery system. Credit: Cummins
Panasonic announced plans
to adapt portions of its Kansas EV battery factory to produce energy storage systems specifically for data centers, highlighting rapid manufacturing diversification beyond automotive applications. The company's rack-mounted systems incorporate multiple storage modules with lithium-ion cells, offering backup functionality and peak shaving capabilities that cover shortages during demand periods.
Market segmentation reveals distinct deployment patterns
Systems ranging from 100 kWh to 1 MWh lead with 38% market share, reflecting suitability for distributed and medium-scale requirements. Hyperscale data centers dominate with 42% share, driven by large power requirements and rapid computing expansion. On-grid systems hold 61% deployment share, supported by utility power integration and energy-management capabilities.
Backup power leads applications with 49% share, though operators increasingly deploy batteries for peak shaving (21%), renewable integration (16%), and grid services (9%). Europe accounts for 27% of the market, driven by renewable-energy integration and grid flexibility requirements, while Asia-Pacific represents 26%, supported by rapid digitalization and hyperscale development.
Related:
Fail-Safe BESS Technology Prevents Thermal Runaway at Single-Cell Level
M&A activity and safety considerations shape the competitive landscape
The mergers and acquisitions landscape reflects market significance. Nextpower agreed to acquire Prevalon Energy for up to $365 million in May 2026, adding large-scale BESS and energy-management capabilities. T1 Energy's June 2026 agreement to acquire KORE Power expands capabilities in battery storage systems, software, and AI data center infrastructure. Brookfield's $7 billion acquisition of Aypa Power in July 2026 provides access to a large North American battery-storage platform.
Technical challenges extend beyond capacity scaling. Battery industry experts emphasize that safety protocols for data center applications must exceed electric vehicle standards. Bringing high-energy-density batteries with flammable chemistries like NMC into data center white space represents significant risk, driving increased adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry offering superior thermal stability and safety characteristics. The transition from passive backup to active power management represents fundamental reimagining of data center power architecture, with BESS solutions becoming essential tools enabling developers to build resilient energy ecosystems supporting faster deployment and reliable operation of hyperscale and AI-driven campuses.

title: Ports deploy battery fleets to cut diesel use
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Battery News
APM Terminals Elizabeth and HHLA TK Estonia have ordered battery-electric terminal trucks and cranes, signaling a move to fleet-scale, full-shift battery operation.
October 4, 2026
4 Min Read
Crains and containers at the Muuga container yard
HHLA TK Estonia
At a Glance
APM Terminals Elizabeth orders 96 electric terminal trucks with 310 kWh batteries from Orange EV maker.
Konecranes delivers first European full-battery RTG cranes with 296 kWh systems to Estonia terminal.
Battery packs enable eight-hour crane shifts and multi-shift truck operations without diesel refueling.
As global trade volumes grow, container terminals face mounting pressure to cut their on-land emissions. Shipping lines have drawn most of the maritime decarbonization spotlight, but many port operators also run large fleets of diesel cargo-handling equipment around the clock.
Within a typical container yard, drivers use terminal trucks to shuttle boxes between ship-to-shore cranes and storage stacks. Operators then use gantry cranes to place those boxes. Because many terminals sit close to residential neighborhoods, nearby residents live with the exhaust and noise that equipment produces.
Electrifying that equipment, however, presents a different engineering problem than electrifying passenger cars.
Terminal operators generally need machines that work through multi-shift schedules with little downtime. Engineers must therefore balance battery capacity, cycle life, and charging strategy to meet that requirement. Operators must also secure enough grid capacity and charging infrastructure to support entire fleets, a sizable investment at sites that operators designed around diesel fueling. For those reasons, many operators have moved cautiously, trialing a few electric units before committing to fleet-wide changes.
Related:
2026 Ford Mustang Mach-E Delivers Range but BlueCruise Falls Short in Testing
Recently, several operators have moved past that caution with larger orders. In this article, we'll take a look at two new orders that bring battery-electric trucks and cranes to terminals in New Jersey and Estonia.
APM Terminals Elizabeth orders 96 electric terminal trucks
In August 2026, Orange EV
announced
that APM Terminals Elizabeth in New Jersey had ordered 96 of its electric terminal trucks, also known as terminal tractors. According to Orange EV, the order marks one of the largest port electrification commitments in history. Before the New Jersey order, APM Terminals had already expanded its Orange EV fleet at APM Terminals Los Angeles (Pier 400). After a year-long pilot with 20 rental trucks, the operator added 40 more trucks there this summer, bringing that fleet to 60.
For the Elizabeth order, APM Terminals selected Orange EV's HUSK-e XP model. Orange EV designed each truck for heavy terminal work, rating it to move up to 180,000 lbs. of combined weight. To power that work, the company equips the trucks with a 310 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, the largest pack in its lineup.
Orange EV and APM Terminals team members. Credit: OrangeEV
Importantly, APM Terminals based the purchase on more than upfront unit cost, according to Orange EV. The operator also weighed uptime, spare parts availability, and service response standards. On uptime, Orange EV reports that its installed fleet averages more than 97% uptime.
Related:
The EV Insurance Penalty Is Over: 6 Models with Major Premium Reductions
Ultimately, Orange EV CEO Kurt Neutgens links the Elizabeth order to the Pier 400 expansion. As he explained, the two orders are “evidence of an inflection point in ports as operators move past the pilot and testing phase.”
Konecranes brings full-shift battery cranes to Estonia
Beyond yard trucks, terminal operators are also targeting diesel use in their cranes. In March 2026, Konecranes
announced
that HHLA TK Estonia had ordered two rubber-tired gantry (RTG) cranes for the Port of Muuga.
Konecranes designed the cranes to run full operational shifts on battery power. According to the company, the order marks the first time it has shipped RTGs with batteries of this scale to Europe. HHLA TK Estonia will use the 1-over-5, six-lane cranes to replace older RTGs, and the Finnish manufacturer plans to deliver the cranes in Q4 2026.
The Muuga container yard. Credit: HHLA TK Estonia
For context, terminal operators in a typical yard drive RTG cranes on rubber tires to straddle and stack rows of containers. Traditionally, manufacturers have powered those cranes with onboard diesel generators. To cut emissions, Konecranes now offers options ranging from renewable diesel and hybrid drives to fully electrified fleets under its Ecolifting roadmap.
Related:
Bentley Unveils Torcal EV With 876 HP, V8-Inspired Drum Sound & 375-Mile Range
Within that range, Konecranes pairs a large battery with fixed charging for the Estonian cranes. The company specified a 296 kWh battery system, which it says enables up to eight hours of independent operation. To recharge the cranes, HHLA TK Estonia will use an integrated 25-meter busbar charging system. According to Konecranes, operators running the cranes fully on battery power eliminate tailpipe emissions during crane operations and reduce yard noise.
Beyond the Muuga deployment, Konecranes regional sales manager Philipp Reiter sees broader significance in the order. As he noted, “This order demonstrates how battery technology is shifting from being a mitigation solution to providing power for full-scale operational use.”
Electrifying the container yard
Overall, port operators are bringing battery technology to two of the main workhorses of the container yard. APM Terminals has moved from a year-long pilot at Pier 400 to a 96-truck order in New Jersey. Meanwhile, HHLA TK Estonia is moving battery cranes into full-shift duty. In each case, the buyers chose large battery packs, with 310 kWh per truck and 296 kWh per crane.
As these fleets grow from pilot units to dozens of machines, terminal operators will face new questions about the infrastructure behind the batteries. They will need to plan grid connections, charging schedules, and energy management with the same care they give berth and crane scheduling. Operators that solve those problems first could set the template for how ports move the world's cargo without diesel.

title: How Kodiak & IKEA are Taking the Driver Out of Freight
content:
How Kodiak & IKEA are Taking the Driver Out of Freight
Prioritise Us
on Google
Kodiak AI is an autonomous vehicle technology company founded in April 2018. Credit: Kodiak
IKEA is becoming the first driverless launch shipper partner for Don Burnette's Kodiak AI, with the founder and CEO eyeing a 2026 Texas launch
IKEA Supply is set to become the first company to move long-haul freight on Kodiak AI's driverless trucks, with no human in the cab, later in 2026.
The autonomous trucking company announced the plan on 29 September 2026, four years after it began hauling IKEA goods in Texas.
Over that period, Kodiak says it has delivered more than 1,300 loads and driven more than 1.2 million kilometres autonomously, with a safety observer on board.
It says the trucks ran seven days a week, day and night, with a “nearly perfect on-time delivery record”.
Key facts:
IKEA Supply will move freight on Kodiak AI's driverless trucks, with no human in the cab, later in 2026.
The first driverless leg covers 352km, mainly along Interstate 45 between Kodiak's Houston and Dallas-area facilities.
That leg is part of a 470km route linking IKEA's distribution centre in Baytown, Texas, with its store in Frisco, Texas.
Kodiak has hauled IKEA goods in Texas for four years, delivering more than 1,300 loads.
Its trucks have driven more than 1.2 million kilometres autonomously on the route, with a safety observer on board.
Driverless trucks on the I-45
The first driverless leg will cover 352km, mainly along Interstate 45 between Kodiak's facilities in Houston and the Dallas area.
It forms part of a 470km route linking IKEA's distribution centre in Baytown, Texas with its store in Frisco, Texas.
Kodiak says it has tested trucks on the same route for four years “without incident”.
In its announcement, the company says: “Unsupervised driverless operations – no human in the cab – represent a milestone the entire Kodiak team has been tirelessly working toward since Kodiak was founded more than eight years ago.”
It adds that it is now “only months away” from that milestone.
Predicting hauling schedules
For a shipper, the value of autonomy lies as much in predictability as in removing the driver.
Kodiak says the partners have learned exactly when and where trucks should be launched, and precisely when they will reach Frisco.
That allows IKEA to schedule unloading at a specific dock door before a truck arrives.
Predictive maintenance data is also used to set a proactive maintenance plan for each truck.
The company says: “This orchestration allows for greater asset utilisation and improved reliability throughout the supply chain.”
A 2021 World Economic Forum whitepaper says trucks in Europe are on the road only 29% of the time.
It cites a 2018 PwC study suggesting
autonomous trucks
could be on the road up to 78% of the time.
We have almost two years experience in driverless operations – no human in the cab – for a paying customer in the Permian Basin.
Don Burnette, Founder and CEO of Kodiak
The same paper estimates that 15% of the distance trucks travel is driven empty.
McKinsey's 2024 report on autonomous trucking says the technology could cut the total cost of ownership of heavy-duty trucks by 42% per mile on long routes.
McKinsey says routes from 320 to 640km only become viable as costs fall.
Safety and long-haul drivers
Before the launch, Kodiak is completing its highway launch safety case for driverless long-haul operations.
The company describes this as a structured, evidence-backed argument that the Kodiak Driver, its autonomous driving system, is safe to run without a human on board in a defined area.
Kodiak also says focusing autonomous trucks on long-haul routes lets human drivers concentrate on the local driving jobs that most of them prefer.
The company says: “They can reduce their time sleeping on the side of the highway and instead be home with family and friends.”
McKinsey estimates the US is
short of more than 80,000 truck drivers
, a gap it expects to double by 2030. In Europe, it says more than 200,000 truck-driving jobs are unfilled.
Scaling driverless freight
Kodiak’s technology uses AWS as its primary cloud provider to support AI development and safety simulations.
“AWS cloud services enhance Kodiak's ability to launch and scale our driverless operations safely and reliably,” says Don Burnette, Founder and CEO of Kodiak.
Don Burnette, Founder and CEO of Kodiak. Credit: Kodiak
The company began its driverless long-haul launch programme in August, which it says consistently completes deliveries between Lancaster, Texas and its launch destination in Houston without human intervention.
When announcing Kodiak’s “driverless launch lane” between Dallas and Houston, the same destination cities IKEA is set to use, Don said: “We have almost two years experience in driverless operations – no human in the cab – for a paying customer in the Permian Basin.”
Atlas Energy Solutions, the customer in question, began using Kodiak’s technology in its owned trucks to haul freight across the Permian Basin in West Texas and Eastern New Mexico in 2024.
Kodiak says the IKEA launch is not a one-off, and that it will continue to scale driverless technology with IKEA and other customers.
McKinsey expects 13% of trucks on US roads to be autonomous by 2035, against 11% in China and 4% in Europe.
Key companies
IKEA Supply
CEO: Jakub Jankowski (CEO of Inter IKEA Group)
Headquarters: Pratteln, Switzerland
IKEA Supply is the main supply company of Inter IKEA Group, the IKEA franchisor and owner of the IKEA brand. It sources, supplies, sells and distributes IKEA products to franchisees worldwide. The wider group, led by CEO Jakub Jankowski since January 2026, makes about 10% of the IKEA range itself and reported total revenues of €26.3bn in FY25.
Kodiak AI
CEO: Don Burnette
Headquarters: California, US
Founded in 2018 by Don Burnette, Kodiak AI develops the Kodiak Driver, a virtual driver system for long-haul, industrial and defence trucking. Listed on Nasdaq since September 2025, it had 35 driverless trucks working in the Permian Basin by June 2026 for Atlas Energy Solutions. IKEA will be its first driverless long-haul customer later in 2026.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is Amazon's cloud computing business, offering computing, storage, database and AI services to start-ups, enterprises and governments. Kodiak uses AWS as its primary cloud provider, running AI development and safety simulations for the Kodiak Driver on its infrastructure. title: CMA CGM Group: Strengthening US Logistics Capabilities
content:
CMA CGM Group: Strengthening US Logistics Capabilities
Prioritise Us
on Google
CMA CGM Group has finalised its acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain. Credit: CMA CGM
CMA CGM Group’s completed acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain is strengthening North American logistics efficiency, explains Rodolphe Saadé, Chairman and CEO
Integrated, end-to-end logistics are facing greater demand than ever, alongside increasing levels of challenges, both external and internal.
In order to make its operations more efficient, CMA CGM Group announced its
plans to acquire FedEx Supply Chain
earlier this year.
Now, that acquisition has been successfully closed, starting a multi-year commercial agreement with air and ocean freight.
Logistics acquisition
The CMA CGM Group is a global player in sea, land, air and logistics solutions. As a global enterprise, it has undergone a period of growth due to a range of external acquisitions. In 1998, it grew its Oceania capabilities with ANL. In 2017, MERCOSUL LINE joined the group, working to make
multimodal transportation more sustainable
CEVA Logistics joined the Group in 2019, offering a comprehensive range of solutions across freight. In 2021, the Group launched its airfreight division, offering regular service, chartered flights and a range of solutions.
Now, it has announced the successful closure of its acquisition of
FedEx Supply Chain
, with a deal totalling US$1.4bn. This reinforces a 25-year commitment to investments in the United States from the Group. It also expands CEVA Logistics’ North American contract logistics operations.
With this expanded network, the company can now reach more customers at a faster rate, meeting demand in a much more efficient manner.
Rodolphe Saadé, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the CMA CGM Group
FedEx Supply Chain has been acquired by CMA GGM Group. Credit: FedEx
Growing capabilities
A FedEx workforce of nearly 10,000 members have now been integrated into CEVA Logistics, making it one of North America’s leading contract logistics providers. Alongside this, the acquisition has tripped the logistics footprint of the company in North America, with an additional 34 million square feet of warehouse space being added to CEVA’s network.
Due to this, the company can store more products and have a wider offering to its customers. CEVA now has approximately 150 warehouses under its ownership, with an expanded presence of more than 240 locations and a workforce of approximately 20,000.
This means that the company can work in a streamlined manner, making use of more manpower and more locations. This helps reduce delivery times and handover errors – as there are more locations, there are more warehouses to choose from, meaning operations can take place in an area closer to the final destination.
completion of this acquisition marks an important
step in the development of CMA CGM and CEVA Logistics in North America,” explains Rodolphe Saadé, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the CMA CGM Group.
“By significantly expanding our contract logistics capabilities, we are strengthening our ability to offer customers integrated, end-to-end supply chain solutions across ocean, air, land and logistics. It also reinforces CMA CGM’s long-term commitment to investing in the United States, a strategic growth market for the Group, and supporting the resilience and efficiency of its supply chain.”
The acquisition also combines digital and operational capabilities, allowing for the greater deployment of automation and robotics across the North American network. As it is expanding its network and gaining deeper access to automation, it is also gaining new expertise in healthcare, technology, consumer and retail.
Through this, it is growing its end-to-end supply chain management capabilities across North America.
Rodolphe Saadé, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the CMA CGM Group
Key numbers
Approximately 10,000 FedEx employees have joined the CMA CGM Group
CEVA has gained 34 million square feet of warehouse space
It now owns approximately 150 warehouses
CEVA operates in more than 240 locations
The deal was at an enterprise value of US$1.4bn
Ongoing collaboration
The acquisition reflects transformation both for CMA CGM Group and for FedEx. FedEx is undertaking a strategy of simplification – reducing complexity in its portfolio and its strategy. In doing this, it is able to focus on the areas where it knows it can create and nurture long-term value.
“Today’s milestone demonstrates the continued progress we are making to execute our strategy with rigor and discipline,” says
Raj Subramaniam, President and Chief Executive Officer of FedEx
“We are building a more focused FedEx, centered on the differentiated capabilities that have made our unparalleled network essential to global commerce. As we continue to strengthen our core transportation network and deepen our reach across high-value verticals, FedEx is simultaneously creating value for our customers and stockholders.
“I want to thank our FedEx Supply Chain team members for their many contributions to FedEx and our customers over the years. We wish them success as they begin their next chapter with CEVA Logistics, and we look forward to continuing our relationship with CMA CGM.”
Alongside the sale of FedEx Supply Chain to CMA CGM Group, the two companies have entered into a multi-year commercial agreement, focusing on air and ocean freight. This allows both companies to unlock new value within global collaboration and trade.
With the new deal, CMA CGM will become the preferred ocean carrier for FedEx and the companies will collaborate on an air cargo capacity agreement.
As a result, there will be greater flexibility on long-haul routes and greater demonstration of
integrated logistics solutions
Raj Subramaniam, CEO of FedEx. Credit: FedEx
Key companies
CEO: Raj Subramaniam
HQ: Tennessee, US
FedEx Corporation is a global leader in transportation, e-commerce, and business services, delivering to more than 220 countries and territories worldwide. With over 500,000 team members, the company operates through multiple divisions including FedEx Express, Ground, Freight, and Services. Under CEO Raj Subramaniam's leadership, FedEx is pursuing a strategic simplification to focus on its core differentiated transportation network capabilities.
CMA CGM Group
CEO: Rodolphe Saadé
HQ: Marseille, France
CMA CGM Group is a global leader in shipping and logistics, founded in 1978 and led by Chairman Rodolphe Saadé. Headquartered in Marseille, France, it operates over 600 vessels serving 420 ports across 160 countries. CMA CGM provides integrated solutions spanning ocean freight, air cargo, inland transportation, and contract logistics, with strong commitment to decarbonization and sustainable shipping operations.
CEO: Patrick Moebel
HQ: Marseille, France
CEVA Logistics is a global supply chain company acquired by CMA CGM Group in 2019. Operating in over 170 countries, it provides freight management and contract logistics solutions across multiple industries. Following the FedEx Supply Chain acquisition, CEVA now operates 150 warehouses across 240+ North American locations with 20,000 employees, establishing itself as a leading regional contract logistics provider.
MERCOSUL LINE
CEO: Eduardo Galo
HQ: Santos, São Paulo, Brazil
MERCOSUL LINE is a multimodal transportation company that joined CMA CGM Group in 2017. Based in South America, it specializes in sustainable logistics solutions across road, rail, and maritime transport. MERCOSUL LINE connects key trade routes throughout Latin America, emphasizing environmental responsibility and operational efficiency. The acquisition strengthened CMA CGM's regional presence while advancing the Group's commitment to sustainable multimodal transportation solutions.

title: IFR: Professional Service Robot Sales Surge 24% Worldwide
content:
IFR: Professional Service Robot Sales Surge 24% Worldwide
Prioritise Us
on Google
117,000 Transport and logistics leads as the top robotics application, according to IFR. Credit: Boston Dynamics
Jane Heffner, President of the IFR, reports 24% growth in professional service robots and 37% in consumer robots as global shipments reach 250,000 units
According to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR), global shipments of professional service robotics increased by 24% to almost 250,000 units last year, highlighting a major shift toward commercial automation across global supply chains.
The IFR published these findings in its World Robotics 2026 report, which shows that 47% of robots sold in 2025 were used for transportation and logistics.
The report also shows that robots were used predominantly in
areas such as hospitality
, professional cleaning, agriculture and inspection and maintenance.
Discussing IFR’s findings, Jane Heffner, President of the International Federation of Robotics, says: “Service robots are expanding into everyday operations.
“Sales went up across all three segments with double-digit growth rates: professional service robots gained 24%, medical robots grew 19% and consumer service robots surged by an impressive 37%.”
Sales went up across all three segments with double-digit growth rates: professional service robots gained 24%, medical robots grew 19% and consumer service robots surged by an impressive 37%.
Jane Heffner, President of the International Federation of Robotics
Key facts
Global shipments of professional service robots increased by 24% to almost 250,000 units in 2025
Transportation and logistics was the leading application for service robotics, accounting for 47% of market share and 117,500 units sold
Consumer service robots saw the highest growth across all three segments, surging by 37%, while medical robots grew by 19%
The humanoid robots sector recorded sales of approximately 7,000 units worldwide in 2025, for commercial and professional applications
Advances in AI, perception systems and autonomous navigation were cited as the key areas driving service robot development
Applications within the robotics market
The leading application for service robotics was transportation and logistics, with 117,500 units sold in 2025. This was up 21%, and represented a market share of 47%.
The majority of the robots sold were used for transportation and for the automation of
material flows
and delivery processes.
While traditional sales remained the primary monetisation channel, RaaS (Robotics as a Service) business models continued to grow in popularity.
In the US, this remained the dominant business model.
In second place were hospitality robots. Machines for mobile guidance, information points in public settings and telepresence accounted for the majority of these robots.
Top 5 application groups for professional use in 2025. Credit: IFR
Robots for cleaning applications ranked in third place, with floor cleaning serving as the main application within this segment.
At the same time, humanoid robots – which are designed to resemble humans and operate in human-focused environments – are gaining popularity in the industry for their potential flexibility.
While recent
advances in AI
, sensors and control systems have resulted in dynamic pilot projects, most current applications remain specialised and still often require human input.
In 2025, the humanoid robots sector – which IFR Chair of the Service Robot Committee Dr. Werner Klaus says is the “newest robotics market” – experienced sales of approximately 7,000 units worldwide. These robots were intended for commercial and professional applications beyond R&D and entertainment purposes.
Considerable challenges such as safety standards, high training and maintenance costs and the lack of justification from a business point of view – particularly in industrial settings – continue to limit widespread adoption.
For humanoid robots to become practical, everyday tools, IFR says further progress in intuitive programming, robust manipulation, economic scaling and standardised safety is essential.
Jane Heffner, President of the International Federation of Robotics. Credit: International Federation of Robotics
Robotics and the human impact
Last month, IFR released a report on the impact service robots are currently having on human life across all global industries.
The report outlines how service robots are
addressing labour shortages
, improving productivity and supporting healthcare, hospitality, cleaning, security and several other sectors.
The report cites advances in AI, perception systems and autonomous navigation as the key areas for service robot development.
It adds that rather than replacing people, robots are supporting employees by taking over repetitive, physically demanding, hazardous or time-consuming tasks, allowing workers to focus on activities that require human judgement, creativity and interpersonal skills.

Headquarters: Zurich, Switzerland
ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, driving software-integrated engineering solutions to optimize manufacturing and robotics performance.
CEO: Christoph Schell
Headquarters: Augsburg, Germany
KUKA is a major global automation supplier specializing in intelligent industrial robots, automated systems, and logistics solutions for smart factories.
Yaskawa Electric Corporation
CEO: Hiroshi Ogasawara
Headquarters: Kitakyushu, Japan
Yaskawa is a pioneer in motion control, AC drives, and mechatronics, manufacturing industrial robots used extensively across global automated production lines.

title: Exploring Supply Chain Automation and Growth at Infios
content:
Exploring Supply Chain Automation and Growth at Infios
Prioritise Us
on Google
Warehouse operations are increasingly integrating the use of robotics. Credit: Getty
As supply chains become increasingly complex, Matt Gregory, SVP Growth EMEA and Global Hardware and Steve Blough, Chief Strategist at Infios share insights
In global supply chains, businesses are beginning to integrate technology into their supply chains more, but finding the balance between human and machine is a fine art.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Matt Gregory, SVP, Growth EMEA and Global Hardware at Infios and Steve Blough, Chief Strategist at Infios about how the company is strengthening its own operations in order to deliver stronger customer service.
1. How do commercial growth in EMEA and global hardware innovation come together at Infios?
They come together around a common objective: helping organisations sense what is happening across their supply chain, make better decisions and turn those decisions into action. My role across EMEA and global hardware gives me a perspective that spans both the strategic challenges customers are facing and how technology, including automation and hardware, can help address them.
Across EMEA, we’re seeing strong demand for greater agility and execution. Customers are operating in an environment shaped by changing consumer expectations, labour constraints, geopolitical uncertainty and continued pressure on costs. They need to be able to respond quickly when conditions change, while maintaining service levels and controlling operational complexity.
That is driving interest in technology that connects different parts of the operation rather than optimising individual processes in isolation. Software, automation, data and AI increasingly need to work together to help organisations understand what is happening, determine the best course of action and execute it effectively.
We’re also seeing a clear shift away from optimising individual parts of the supply chain in isolation. Customers want to connect the signals across their operations so they can understand what is happening, make better decisions and act quickly when conditions change. That means connecting order, warehouse and transportation processes, while increasingly
bringing AI and automation
into the execution layer.
Ultimately, the opportunity is to move from reactive supply chains to adaptive ones. That is the thinking behind Intelligent Supply Chain Execution at Infios: using connected data, AI and orchestration to help organisations sense change, make better decisions and take the right action at the right time, while learning from outcomes to continuously improve how the supply chain responds to what happens next.
Matt Gregory, SVP, Growth EMEA and Global Hardware at Infios. Credit: Infios
2. How have acquisitions and internal growth strengthened your ability to meet customer demand?
The real value of that evolution is not simply that we have added more capabilities. It is that we can bring together different parts of the supply chain that have traditionally been managed separately, helping customers connect the digital flow of orders and information with the physical flow of goods.
Our heritage in warehouse execution and automation, combined with the capabilities added in recent years through enVista, MercuryGate and more recently vaibe, gives us a broader perspective across
Order Management, Warehouse Management and Transportation Management
. That allows us to look at how a decision in one part of the supply chain affects execution somewhere else, whether that is inventory availability, warehouse capacity, labour, transportation or the movement of goods.
That connection is becoming increasingly important as supply chains become more dynamic. Robotics, transportation systems, AI and other technologies can each deliver value, but the real opportunity comes when they operate as part of a coordinated execution environment rather than as individual investments.
That is the foundation of Intelligent Supply Chain Execution at Infios. We’re focused on connecting the signals, decisions and actions across the supply chain so organisations can sense what is changing, decide how to respond, act with greater speed and precision, and learn from the outcome. The result is a supply chain that can continuously adapt rather than simply execute a plan that may already be out of date.
3. How are your customers approaching automation and voice technology?
The conversation has definitely moved beyond automation for automation’s sake. Customers are increasingly asking a much more practical question: where can automation make a measurable difference to the performance of my operation?
We’re seeing business-critical deployments across areas such as robotics, voice and other forms of warehouse automation, particularly where organisations are dealing with labour constraints, increasing volumes or the need for greater accuracy and consistency. The most mature organisations are no longer treating automation as an isolated innovation project; it is becoming an integral part of how the operation runs.
That said, maturity varies significantly between organisations. Some are scaling established technologies, while others are still validating particular use cases or working through the integration and change-management challenges that come with automation. What is increasingly clear, however, is that the greatest value comes when automation is connected to the wider flow of the supply chain. A warehouse should not operate in isolation from Order Management or Transportation Management. If demand changes, for example, the warehouse may need to adjust fulfilment priorities while transportation responds to changes in capacity or delivery requirements.
That is where Infios Archer becomes particularly relevant. As the intelligence layer powering Infios AI, Infios Archer brings together data and context across Order Management, Warehouse Management and Transportation Management, helping turn what is happening across the operation into actionable intelligence. Rather than automation simply executing predefined tasks, Infios Archer can help identify changes, determine what needs to happen next and coordinate the appropriate response across connected workflows. This creates a more continuous sense, decide, act and learn cycle across the supply chain.
Ultimately, the value of automation is not measured by how much technology an organisation deploys, but by the business outcomes it enables. When software, AI, automation and people work together, organisations can respond faster to changing conditions, improve productivity and accuracy, and continuously learn from how the operation performs. That is the shift towards Intelligent Supply Chain Execution: using intelligence to make the supply chain more adaptive, responsive and capable of improving over time.
Infios solutions include a range of sorting robots. Credit: Infios
4. How do you ensure AI and automation are working seamlessly together, rather than as isolated silos?
The starting point is to stop thinking about AI, automation and software as separate technology projects. They need to be considered in the context of the operational decisions and workflows they are there to improve.
That means connecting Order Management, Warehouse Management and Transportation Management, while also connecting the physical technologies such as robotics, voice and other automation into that same execution environment. The intelligence needs to understand the operational context, not simply process data in isolation.
This is where an intelligence layer becomes important. Infios Archer, the intelligence layer powering Infios AI, brings together operational data and context across the execution environment so AI can do more than identify an issue. It can help determine what that issue means, recommend or initiate the appropriate response, and learn from the outcome. The objective is to create a continuous sense, decide, act and learn cycle without requiring users to understand how the underlying technology or application architecture. In practical terms, that means the logisticians can focus on applying their expertise to the supply chain rather than having to navigate the complexity of the technology supporting it. That becomes increasingly important as AI capabilities span more solutions and become more deeply embedded across the overall supply chain.
The test of an intelligent supply chain, therefore, isn't
how much AI or automation a company has deployed
. It is whether those technologies are helping the operation make better decisions and execute them more effectively. When they are connected to the workflows and systems people use every day, AI and automation become part of the way the supply chain operates rather than another layer of technology for teams to manage.
Steve Blough, Chief Strategist at Infios. Credit: Infios
5. Can you share an example of where Infios has helped a customer solve a specific bottleneck?
A good example is our work with Spirit Halloween, which operates one of the most complex seasonal retail models in the industry. Every year, the company opens more than 1,400 temporary stores and then faces an enormous surge in demand around its October peak. Heading into one of its biggest peak seasons, Spirit was also dealing with tariff uncertainty, tightening logistics capacity and legacy fulfilment systems that were being pushed to their limits.
The challenge was not simply handling more orders. Spirit needed greater visibility and coordination across its retail, e-commerce and marketplace operations, while also improving its Buy Online, Pick Up In Store (BOPIS) performance. The business needed to be able to prepare for disruption rather than simply react when it arrived.
We worked with Spirit to connect Infios Order Management and Warehouse Management, creating a more unified flow of information between order orchestration,
inventory and fulfilment
. Infios OM provides real-time order orchestration and intelligent inventory allocation, while Infios WM improves operational and labour efficiency and gives the business greater visibility into inventory. Connecting those capabilities allows information to flow between the order and warehouse environments in real time, helping Spirit execute against demand as it changes.
The results demonstrate why that connection matters. Spirit reduced BOPIS rejection rates from 7% to 3.3%, while processing two million transactions through Infios OM in a single day. During peak season, more than 1.6 million orders were fulfilled.
What I think is particularly important is that Spirit wasn't simply looking to add another system. It needed the technology to support the way its business actually operates: extreme seasonality, rapidly changing demand and a combination of physical stores and e-commerce channels. By connecting Order Management and Warehouse Management, Spirit was able to create a much more coordinated execution environment and maintain performance even under significant supply chain and tariff pressures.
It also illustrates an important point about Intelligent Supply Chain Execution. The value comes from connecting the signals across the operation so that organisations can understand what is happening, make better decisions and act quickly. In Spirit's case, that meant connecting order and inventory information with warehouse execution to keep fulfilment moving at extraordinary volumes.
That connected foundation is also what enables organisations to introduce greater intelligence over time. When order, inventory and execution data are connected,
AI can be applied in the context
of the operation rather than in isolation – helping organisations sense changes, understand their impact, determine what needs to happen next and ultimately learn from how the supply chain responds.
For me, the Spirit Halloween example is a good illustration of where supply chain execution is heading. It isn't about deploying technology for its own sake. It is about creating an environment where systems, data, people and, increasingly, AI can work together to help the operation respond to whatever demand, disruption or opportunity comes next.
Infios worked with Spirit Halloween to improve operations. Credit: Spirit Halloween
6. What do you see as the biggest opportunities and pitfalls regarding modular supply chain tech?
The biggest opportunity with modularity is that it allows organisations to evolve their supply chain at the pace of the business. They can address the most important constraint or opportunity today, demonstrate value and then extend their capabilities as requirements change. That is particularly important when supply chains are having to adapt to new customer expectations, labour constraints, automation requirements and increasingly unpredictable operating conditions.
But modularity only works if the modules can work together. The biggest pitfall is creating a collection of technically independent solutions that each optimise a particular process but leave the organisation responsible for stitching everything together. You can end up with more interfaces, more data hand-offs and more complexity, essentially recreating the silos you were trying to remove.
The other mistake is starting with the technology rather than the business outcome. Organisations should first identify where execution needs to improve and then determine which capabilities they need to address it. Modularity should give them choice and flexibility without sacrificing a coherent operating model.
For me, the ideal architecture is one where capabilities can be introduced and evolved independently, but still share the data, context and intelligence needed to execute as one supply chain. We often talk about the supply chain as if it were a homogeneous environment, but in reality it is highly complex, with different products, services, processes and customer requirements all operating within the same network. That
makes adaptability critical
. Solutions need to be configurable rather than reliant on custom coding, so organisations can respond to disruption, changing requirements and new opportunities without constantly rebuilding their technology.
That is where modularity becomes much more than a technology strategy. It becomes a way to continuously improve execution: adding new capabilities, including AI and automation, without having to rethink the entire architecture every time something changes.

title: Toyota gets the green light for a new EV built to take on China
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 5 2026 - 8:57 am PT
will invest around $1.3 billion, the largest in Argentina’s automotive industry to date, to produce a new electric vehicle at its site in Buenos Aires.
Toyota plans to build a new EV in Argentina
Toyota Argentina announced it had received approval from the Evaluation Committee to join the RIGI (Incentive Regime for Large Investments) to produce a new electric vehicle at its plant in Zárate, Buenos Aires province.
The project will cost around $1.3 billion, Toyota said, making it the largest investment in Argentina’s auto industry ever.
Toyota has been producing vehicles at the facility since 1997. The new investment will create around 3,600 jobs during the initial construction phase and about 2,600 once the upgrades are complete.
The site currently produces Toyota vehicles, including the Hilux pickup, SW4 SUV, and Hiace commercial van.
Toyota said it will announce more details shortly, including production plans. According to
Automotive News
, Toyota’s all-electric pickup, the Hilux BEV, is a likely candidate for production in Argentina.
Toyota Hilux BEV (Source: Toyota)
Toyota currently builds the Hilux EV in Thailand and exports it to Europe, Asia, Australia, and other overseas markets.
The announcement comes as Chinese brands like BYD, Geely, and Chery dominate EV sales in Latin America with lower-cost vehicles.
Toyota Hilux BEV pickup models (Source: Toyota Australia)
BYD sold 85,800 vehicles in Latin America through July, according to MarkLines. That’s nearly 60% of the region’s 147,493 electric vehicles sold in the same period.
Argentina’s Minister of Economy, Luis Caputo, said Toyota’s plant would generate around $1.28 billion in annual exports, with about 70% of production dedicated to foreign markets.
Electrek’s Take
Toyota’s “multi-pathway” strategy calls for offering all powertrain options, including gas, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, battery electric, and fuel cell electric vehicles.
As Chinese brands like BYD gain market share in key global markets such as Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Europe, Toyota is being forced to adapt.
Breaking with its traditional approach, Toyota, like many global OEMs, is
increasingly relying on Chinese batteries
, software, and other vehicle components to compete globally.
Toyota broke ground on a new Lexus EV manufacturing plant in Shanghai last summer. The facility, set to open in 2027, will move at “Lexus speed,” the company calls it, using advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up output.

title: Gas cars fall below 50% of global new car sales for the first time
content:
Gas cars are now a minority of the world’s new car sales. Gasoline-only vehicles made up 49% of global new-vehicle sales in the first half of 2026, down from 73% in 2021, according to Mobility Global data first reported by Nikkei.
It’s the first time on record that they’ve been under half. But there’s a catch: most of the cars taking their place still have a gas tank.
Gas cars lost 24 points of share in under five years
Mobility Global is the auto data firm formerly known as S&P Global Mobility, which was spun off from S&P Global this year. Nikkei reported its first-half numbers last week, and they show sales of gasoline-only cars down 10% from a year ago to 20.25 million units between January and June.
Their share fell three points in a single year, from 52% to 49%.
Battery-electric vehicles grew 12% to 6.87 million units and took 17% of the market, up three points. Conventional hybrids grew 10% to 7.27 million units, or 18%.
| Powertrain | H1 2026 sales | Change | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gasoline-only | 20.25 million | -10% | 49% |
| Hybrid | 7.27 million | +10% | 18% |
| Battery-electric | 6.87 million | +12% | 17% |
| Diesel, plug-in hybrid and other | not reported | not reported | about 16% |
That last row is our math. The reported shares add up to 84%, and the rest is diesel, plug-in hybrids and a few minor fuels.
Nikkei ties the acceleration to oil. Fuel prices spiked with the conflict in the Middle East, and buyers went looking for lower running costs.
The whole car market shrank about 5% in the first half, according to the IEA, so gas-only sales fell twice as fast as the market.
Gas car sales dropped the most in China, down 26%, followed by Europe at 13%. That matches what we’ve been reporting from both markets. In China, sales of gas cars and conventional hybrids fell 40% in August while battery-electric sales edged up. In the EU, ACEA’s registration data has battery-electric cars ahead of petrol cars for the year through August, 1,641,333 to 1,634,733, with petrol down 18.6%.
The EV numbers by region show where the growth is. Mobility Global has battery-electric sales up 32% in Europe to 1.81 million, up 81% in Southeast Asia to 350,000, and more than doubling in Oceania to 110,000. China was down 3% at 3.44 million, which is still half of the world’s total. North America was down 15%.
Yoshiaki Kawano, an associate director at Mobility Global, told Nikkei that few EV buyers go back to gasoline cars or hybrids. He expects demand based on “genuine consumer needs rather than subsidies” to grow as prices come down.
That lines up with the CDK study we covered in July, in which 94% of EV owners said they won’t go back to gas.
83% of new cars still have an engine
“Gas cars under 50%” is accurate, but you have to read the label. The 49% covers cars that run on gasoline and nothing else.
Hybrids are counted separately, and they outsold battery-electric vehicles in the first half, 7.27 million to 6.87 million. A hybrid is a gas car that uses less gas. Diesels and plug-in hybrids sit in the other 16%.
Only the 17% that’s battery-electric burns no fuel at all. So about 83% of the new vehicles sold in the world this year still came with an engine.
It’s also a six-month number, taken in the middle of an oil shock. We’ll see if the full year stays under 50%, but the trend may be accelerating.
The US isn’t going back to gas either
The Mobility Global data got passed around a lot over the weekend, often with a note that the US is the exception and that gas cars are regaining ground here since the federal tax credit ended.
EV sales did take a hit. Cox Automotive expects about 239,000 new EV sales in the third quarter, roughly 6% of the market and down about 45% from the 437,000 sold a year ago, when buyers rushed to beat the September 30 deadline. Just last week, Ford reported that its EV sales fell 80% in the quarter.
But those buyers didn’t go back to gas-only cars. Here’s Cox’s US powertrain mix for the second quarter:
| Powertrain | Q2 2025 | Q2 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Gas and diesel (ICE) | 77.6% | 76.8% |
| Hybrid | 13.0% | 16.3% |
| Battery-electric | 7.4% | 5.8% |
| Plug-in hybrid | 2.0% | 1.1% |
Hybrid volume was up 23%, and 16.3% is a record. The ICE share went down, not up. Electrified vehicles as a whole went from 22.4% to 23.2% of the market.
Cox also has gasoline back around $4.50 a gallon, up 41% from a year ago.
Electrek’s Take
Top comment by John Donovan
“Gas-only cars went from 73% to 49% of the market in less than five years, and nothing in the data suggests they’re getting that share back. ”
Hybrids without a plug still run 100% on gas. Yes, they might be a little more efficient than a gas car of the same weight, but they’re still “gas only” cars.
This is a real milestone, and I don’t want to undersell it. Gas-only cars went from 73% to 49% of the market in less than five years, and nothing in the data suggests they’re getting that share back. The last time gasoline wasn’t on top was the early 1900s, when steam and electric cars outsold it in the US.
I hate seeing media headlines claiming that “EV sales are down” and that “EV growth has stalled.”
The data is clear: that’s true in the US, but only in the US. The rest of the world is moving to electric vehicles, and it is not slowing down.

title: Lucid's $50,000 Cosmos spotted testing in California after 2027 delay
content:
Lucid Motors
lucid cosmos
Fred Lambert
| Oct 5 2026 - 7:34 am PT
Credit: u/always_trolled on Reddit
The Lucid Cosmos is out testing in California traffic. A camouflaged prototype of the midsize SUV was photographed on Highway 101 in Morgan Hill, about 40 miles south of Lucid’s headquarters in Newark.
The four photos show the sub-$50,000 SUV from the rear and the side. They come two months after Lucid pushed the Cosmos launch back to the second half of 2027.
Lucid Cosmos prototype spotted on Highway 101
Reddit user
u/always_trolled
the photos on the Lucid subreddit
. Highway signs in the shots for downtown Morgan Hill, East Dunne Avenue, and Cochrane Road put the prototype northbound on US-101, heading toward San Jose.
A Lucid Cosmos prototype on US-101 in Morgan Hill, California (Credit:
u/always_trolled on Reddit
The car wears California plates and a black, white, and grey wrap made of jumbled letters. Not that the wrap hides much.
The roofline drops sharply toward the back, a spoiler sits at the base of the rear glass, and thin red light strips peek out from a covered panel that runs the width of the tailgate. That lines up with
the Cosmos design Lucid registered in Europe in June
The Cosmos prototype from the side, with flush door handles and a green light on the B-pillar (Credit:
u/always_trolled on Reddit
a Cosmos prototype was photographed next to a Tesla Model Y
near Lucid’s factory in Casa Grande, Arizona.
announced the Cosmos in March
with a 69 kWh battery pack, 300 miles of range, and a starting price under $50,000. The company claims efficiency of 4.5 miles per kWh and 200 miles of range added in 14 minutes. It uses Atlas, Lucid’s new drive unit, which has 30% fewer parts and costs 37% less than the current one.
Lucid Cosmos launch slips to late 2027
Production was supposed to start in late 2026. In August, new CEO Silvio Napoli
pushed the Cosmos to 2027
, “most likely the second half.”
“We’re not going to make the mistake of the past where products, great cars, were in fact tainted by launching before things were ready,” Napoli said.
Lucid needs this car. The company
laid off 18% of its staff in June
, its second deep cut in four months, and
its stock crashed 40% in July on a bankruptcy report that Lucid denied
. It says it has enough liquidity to last well into 2027.
And the competition isn’t waiting. Rivian started building the R2 in April, and
its $45,000 base version is due in late 2027
, the same window Lucid is now targeting for the Cosmos.
Electrek’s Take
A wrapped prototype on a highway isn’t big news by itself, but we are keeping a close eye on this program as it will make or break Lucid in our opinion.
We think Napoli made the right call on the delay. When we
reviewed the Gravity earlier this year
, the hardware was excellent and the software wasn’t ready. Lucid can’t repeat that with a car that has to sell in volume to buyers who are a lot less forgiving than early adopters.
The problem is the timing. Lucid says its liquidity lasts well into 2027, and the Cosmos comes in the second half of 2027. So the car that’s supposed to turn Lucid into a volume automaker shows up around the time its current cash is supposed to run out. That means another check from Saudi Arabia’s PIF, or maybe Uber, before the first customer delivery.
And the product is worth saving. Lucid claims the Cosmos is 10% more efficient than its closest competitor, and efficiency is how you get 300 miles out of a 69 kWh pack and a price under $50,000. Lucid’s powertrains are the most efficient in the business, and we’d love to see what they can do with a more mass-market vehicle.

title: Hyundai's electric hatch goes on sale with up to 308 miles of range, starting at about $25,000
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 5 2026 - 7:14 am PT
The IONIQ 3 has received more interest than any
vehicle in the UK ever. Starting at about $25,000, Hyundai’s electric hatch undercuts much of the competition.
How much does the Hyundai IONIQ 3 cost in the UK?
Hyundai opened orders for the highly anticipated IONIQ 3 in the UK and Europe, its first compact electric vehicle under the IONIQ branding.
The response so far has been “extraordinary,” Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, said after launching the new IONIQ 3 on Monday.
According to Andrew, the electric hatch has received “more customers registering their interest before launch than any new Hyundai we’ve introduced in the UK.” With the full £3,750 Electric Car Grant available on every trim, the IONIQ 3 is one of the most affordable, long-range EVs on the market.
The IONIQ 3 is now available to order in the UK, starting at just £18,495 OTR, or roughly $25,000, including the grant.
It’s available with two battery packs: 42 kWh and 61 kWh. The base IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the 42 kWh battery starts at £18,495 OTR and offers up to 213 miles of WLTP range.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 N-Line (Source: Hyundai UK)
The extended-range IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery starts at £21,995 ($29,000) and offers a “class-leading” WLTP range of up to 308 miles. That also includes the UK government ECG grant.
Hyundai is offering leases from £355 a month for the IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery. The offer is with a £355 deposit and 8.9% APR, including the £3,750 Electric Car Grant
At that, Hyundai’s electric hatch is cheaper than much of the competition, including the Renault 5 E-Tech, priced from £21,495 in the UK, including the ECG. It also undercuts BYD’s new plug-in Dolphin G DM-i (£23,990).
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai said that those who already placed an order can convert their reservation into a full order and receive the full £3,750 Electric Car Grant instead of the previous £1,500 Hyundai Reservation Saving.
The IONIQ 3 measures 4,155 mm (163.5″) in length, 1,800 mm (70.9″) in width, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) in height, with a wheelbase of 2,680 mm (105.5″), which is even a bit smaller than the Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.3.
While it’s under the IONIQ brand, the electric hatch features a distinct new “Aero Hatch” silhouette that maximizes efficiency with a drag coefficient of just 0.263. With a total boot capacity of up to 441 liters, Hyundai said the IONIQ 3 “sets the benchmark in the segment.”
Hyundai IONIQ 3 N-Line interior (Source: Hyundai UK)
The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its new Pleos Connect infotainment system.
Based on the Android Automotive OS platform, Hyundai’s new system is more like using a smartphone. It offers apps and customizable screens, similar to Tesla models. It’s available with a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.
Hyundai’s SmartSense driver assistance technology, Hyundai Digital Key 2, Plug & Charge, an integrated EV Route planner, and Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) all come as standard.
Unlike the IONIQ 5, which uses 800V, the IONIQ 3 uses a 400V architecture. With DC fast charging, the 42 kWh battery can still recharge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes. The 61 kWh battery takes about a minute longer, at around 30 minutes.

Unfortunately, Hyundai has no plans to bring the IONIQ 3 to the US. The compact EV is designed and produced in Europe for European buyers.
